query: For high-entropy nanoalloys in high-temperature applications, what governs structural and chemical stability, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, propose a controlled comparison that would distinguish it from alternatives, predict observations relative to a baseline, define the boundaries of the prediction, identify supporting evidence from the background, and state a falsifying outcome.

generation.hypothesis: For high-entropy nanoalloys made by ultrafast, laser‐induced thermionic emission reduction, the coupling of rapid kinetic trapping with stabilizing interactions from a defective carbon support governs the retention of an equiatomic, disordered structure at high temperatures. This dual action slows atomic diffusion and phase segregation, preserving both the structural and chemical homogeneity that is critical for high-temperature performance.
generation.material_initial_state: Ultrafine (1–3 nm) high-entropy nanoalloys with uniform equiatomic distribution synthesized via laser-induced thermionic emission reduction and dispersed on a defective carbon support.
generation.intervention: Subjecting the nanoalloys to controlled high-temperature annealing (up to roughly 0.5 Tm) in an inert atmosphere.
generation.conditions: Experiments comparing samples made via rapid laser synthesis on defective carbon versus conventionally prepared nanoalloys or those deposited on non-defective supports, under identical heating rates and inert conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The defective carbon support that anchors metal atoms and the rapid cooling kinetics that ‘freeze in’ a disordered atomic arrangement.
generation.mechanism: Rapid synthesis via laser pulses induces fast reduction and cooling, kinetically trapping the high-entropy, equiatomic distribution before significant diffusion can occur, while defects on the carbon support interact with metal atoms to further inhibit their mobility. This cooperative effect reduces the tendency for phase segregation and chemical ordering even when elevated thermal energy might otherwise drive diffusion and structural rearrangement.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under high-temperature annealing, nanoalloys synthesized by this rapid method on defective carbon will maintain their single-phase, homogeneous structure with minimal phase segregation, in contrast to conventionally prepared samples (or those on inert supports) which will show measurable chemical ordering or phase separation.
generation.baseline: Nanoalloys prepared by slower, conventional reduction methods or supported on non-defective substrates typically exhibit onset of phase segregation and chemical ordering when heated under similar conditions.
generation.boundary: This prediction is expected to hold for nanoalloy particles in the ultrafine regime (<5 nm) and for annealing temperatures up to approximately half the melting temperature (0.5 Tm). Beyond these conditions, diffusion-driven segregation may overcome the kinetic trapping and support interactions.
generation.uncertainty: Exact temperature thresholds, time scales required to see segregation, and the quantitative effect of the carbon support’s defect density remain to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two series of high-entropy nanoalloy samples: one via ultrafast laser-induced thermionic emission reduction on a defective carbon support and a control series using a conventional slow reduction method or on a non-defective support. Subject both series to identical high-temperature annealing (in an inert atmosphere) with controlled ramp rates and holding times. Use in situ techniques (such as XRD, TEM, and EDS mapping) to monitor phase composition and elemental distribution.
measurements: Transmission electron microscopy imaging for nanostructural changes
Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy for verifying uniform chemical distribution
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the rapidly synthesized, carbon-supported nanoalloys do not show statistically significant improved structural/chemical stability (i.e., similar or worse phase segregation and chemical ordering compared to the controls) under high-temperature annealing, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Nanoalloys, especially high-entropy nanoalloys (HENAs) that contain equal stoichiometric metallic elements in each nanoparticle, are widely used in vast applications. Currently, the synthesis of HENAs is challenged by slow reaction kinetics that leads to phase segregation, sophisticated pretreatment of precursors, and inert conditions that preclude scalable fabrication of HENAs. Here, we report direct conversion of metal salts to ultrafine HENAs on carbonaceous support by nanosecond pulsed laser under atmospheric conditions. Because of the unique laser-induced thermionic emission and etch on carbon, the reduced metal elements were gathered to ultrafine HENAs and stabilized by defective carbon support. This scalable, facile, and low-cost method overcomes the immiscible issue and can produce various HENAs uniformly with a size of 1 to 3 nanometers and metal elements up to 11 with productivity up to 7 grams per hour. One of the senary HENAs exhibited excellent catalytic performance in oxygen reduction reaction, manifesting great potential in practical applications. Scalable fabriction of ultrasmall high-entropy nanoalloys is realized by laser-induced thermionic emission reduction.

Metal nanoalloys are critical catalysts and widely used in many chemical reactions ranging from environmental to energy fields (). Conventional bottom-up routes, such as wet-chemistry methods for the synthesis of metal nanoalloys, usually need to consider the miscibility of each metallic element in the phase diagrams to avoid the phase segregation during the formation of the particles (). The immiscible issue of metals restricts the realm of nanoalloys and precludes the discovery of new nanoalloys with superior functionalities (). In recent years, high-entropy nanoalloys (HENAs) containing equal stoichiometric ratios of various metals in each particle in a well-mixed manner have attracted a lot of interest because of their unusual physical and chemical properties. These unique properties make them attractive as catalysts (), such as oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) that has great potential for applications in energy and environmental science. Recent studies have revealed that the slow reaction kinetics in traditional methods is one of the major obstacles that lead to the phase segregation in nanoalloys (, ).
